utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Defence had a preliminary issue to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. Thank you. Mr. Mladic is expecting one visit tomorrow morning, so he kindly asks to be late for the trial. We can continue the trial, only he would prefer to receive since that's the minister of justice from Serbia visiting him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What does it mean "late"? Would that be after the second session or after the -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The visit is scheduled for 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then depends on how long the visit takes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The visit should take only half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: An hour and a half, which means --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only half an hour, which means that with a bit of luck Mr. Mladic could be with us after the first session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which we resume usually at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's Mr. Mladic's right to be present, but if he waives that right then of course we would proceed without him. And I take it that there are ways to inform him precisely about what happened in court during his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I take it also that he signs a waiver form tomorrow, which is the usual way of putting it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll arrange it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if there's no other preliminaries, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time to inform the parties about the rescheduling of Witness RM009. Witness RM009 was scheduled to testify via videolink next week, Friday. The Prosecution has informed the Chamber that the testimony will take more than one day. The first two witnesses of next week will most likely take five days, and for that reason the Prosecution will move Witness RM009 to another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rose, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I take it you do have a hard copy of your statement before you? [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] Please turn to paragraph 63. There you say: "On 19 March 1994 I sent two letters of protest to Dr. Karadzic. The first related to BSA harassment of a UN convoy." The question is this: In your view, what did this harassment amount to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the specific incident, but normally harassment meant stopping the convoy unnecessarily or turning it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that the Serbs had the right, according to the protocols that had been signed, to inspect convoys?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the original agreement was made at a time when I was not in Bosnia was that there was full and free movement of all convoys and that the right of inspection was only given subsequent to that. And it was not necessarily part of the original agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter number 9643 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we are about to see a document of the 9th of February, 1994, which is approximately at the beginning of your tour in Bosnia. We're interested in the last paragraph of the document, so the very bottom of the document; the last paragraph on this B/C/S page and the last paragraph on the next page in English. There you see as part of this order by the Main Staff of the VRS that it is ordered as follows: "All planned and authorised convoys should be allowed to cross Republika Srpska territory after inspection." Does it mean and was it the case in practice that there were unscheduled or unplanned convoys which moved without having been announced? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The system of convoy runs was very carefully co-ordinated with all the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any cases where in such conveys there were goods that had not been announced or stated as present?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you exclude the possibility that something like that happened?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly mistakes could have been made in manifesting convoys, but there was certainly no deliberate desire to misstate the goods that were being carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said the following: In cases that the goods that were being transported are not in accordance with the cargo manifest, that in that case blame could not be placed on the side of Republika Srpska if it decided to keep such cargo or turn it back?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such an approach would have been an example of the undue bureaucratic approach taken by the Bosnian Serb side in order to harass, prevent, and stop the free running of convoys, which had been the original intention. The fact there may have been a baked bean tin too many on a convoy was no reason for starving the people for whom that convoy was designed. And I should remind the Court that there were some 600.000 Serbs daily dependent on the receipt of those convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, would you refrain from showing material to anyone in this courtroom. No, you were showing a book which you are not supposed to do. I'll consider with my colleagues what the consequences are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further violation, whatever slight, will have consequences. And this is another example on the record. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I was interested in your view - and I believe it was UNPROFOR view as well - that you blamed the Serb side for UNPROFOR mistakes as well; in other words, if UNPROFOR failed to meet its obligations in terms of properly filling in the paperwork, you found it to be a Serb mistake if such convoys were not let through. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that interpretation. There was no need in the original agreement for a system and inspection of manifests and the matching of those manifests with the cargos. The practice had been extended as a result of a courtesy given before my time to the Serb side to allow them to look at the cargos that were being carried. I would not have allowed that to have happened had it not have already occurred because it was beyond what had originally been agreed with the warring parties, which was the free running of all convoys, aid convoys, throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that at the moment of inspection or control -- actually, inspection, the Serb side had the right to do that, irrespective of what was in the original document. When you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serb side had the right to inspect convoys; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a courtesy that had been extended to the Serb side; it was not a right, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move to paragraph 69 next, please. There -- well, it's a short paragraph to start with: I met with General Delic that evening and he was not interested in a cease-fire at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. Such position of the Muslim side remained in place until the very end of the war, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time the Muslims had already been promised that they were to be given a much larger territory than they had held until then. Since already by the end of 1993 a plan had already been in existence that Serbs were to be left with only 49 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina territory out of over 70 per cent, which is the size of territory that they had under their control at the time. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was certainly aware that there was the discussion about whether the Serb side should have 51 per cent, which I think was their demand, or whether they should have 49 per cent, but the situation was much more complicated than that because of course the Serb side wanted contiguous territory and they also wanted a number of high-value areas, which was not agreed by either the Bosnian government side or the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you have said yourself, on one side there were Muslims and Western powers, and on the other side the Serbs, when it comes to the percentage negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess that was probably the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move to paragraph 70, please. It reads -- well, you quote -- actually, you seem to have been shown a document of the 7th of April, 1994: "... signed by Major-General Manojlo Milovanovic and sent it to the commands of Herzegovina Corps, Drina Corps, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and Tactical Group Visegrad." In the order General Milovanovic states that we should abstain from using any further the assets that we have in the urban part of Gorazde without any artillery destruction of the town and no ill-treatment of the civil population especially with no ill-treatment of foreigners. It is 65 ter 9326. What I have just read out is on page 2. Perhaps we could see that in e-court. We can see from that, since you've already seen the document, that the Serb forces refrained from opening fire on the town of Gorazde. My question is this -- well, we need page 2 for that. Did you know at the time that the Muslim forces from the protected area of Gorazde carried out offensive operations against both VRS positions as well as against Serb civilians. Following such operations, they always went back to the protected area of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no reports from either the UNMOs of that occurrence or, indeed, when the JCOs arrived did they report such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try to jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need 1D549 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is the 6th of October, 2010, transcript of your testimony. The page we are looking for is transcript page from the Karadzic trial, the number being 7375. It is page 56 in e-court, lines 10 through 13. Perhaps my question was not sufficiently clear and I was not specific time-wise, but in this testimony you were asked the following question: [In English] "You were aware of the fact that the Muslim Army had expelled Serbs, and killed quite a few, at that, and they burned their houses in and around Gorazde. You saw the houses, didn't you? "A. I did."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're confusing two time-periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I apologised at the beginning of this question, so --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my time there, I did not have reports, specific reports, of those activities that you mentioned, although indeed they could have been happening and it would have been typical, given what was happening around Srebrenica, for that sort of activity to have occurred. But I had no specific knowledge because we had -- the UNMOs did not report it and we had not deployed the JCOs at that time into Gorazde, who would have reported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When did you send eight of your members to Gorazde? They were also members of the SAS, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were JCOs. Where their original units had been, I don't know. They were JCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They had been trained to plot targets and guide planes to such targets; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't know. If I could just explain to the Court that I was there as a United Nations officer. I was not directly commanding any units from the troop-contributing nations. And therefore, what the skills and capabilities of those troops that had been deployed in Bosnia were, I had no specific knowledge. They were there to help the United Nations Protection Force to deliver humanitarian aid; they were not there in a war-fighting role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rose, in order to have a transcript which is understood by outsiders as well, could you tell us what JCOs are in full and not just use the acronym?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The joint commission officers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- were deployed by the troop-contributing nations as a request -- as a result of a request by me, because I did not have confidence in the quality of the -- or timeliness of the reporting from the United Nations Military Observers that were a separate force to the UNPROFOR force deployed in Bosnia. I needed accurate assessments by military people as to what was happening on the ground; this was not being provided reliably by the United Nations Military Observers. The background and capabilities of the people who were deployed as joint commission officers was a matter for the troop-contributing nations, not for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're explaining it. You went beyond what I ask you because I think we find that in your statement, but for the public who's listening, they now know that it's joint commission officers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When a target was attacked, as was the case in 1993 around Gorazde, how were such targets chosen? Was it supposed to be someone in the field to determine such targets?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there in 1993 and I have no knowledge of any such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But in 1994 --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in 1994 the joint commission officers reported to the headquarters in Sarajevo the details of the attack that was being launched on that time from the Serb side, and as a result of those attacks and the identification from where those attacks were coming, NATO air-strikes were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. But in order for NATO aircraft to know what they're targeting, someone on the ground has to tell them that; right? Somebody on the ground has to guide them to this target? And was that one of those eight persons that you sent out there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The decision to attack Serb positions around Gorazde was your own; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly me that called for the air-strikes, but of course I was part of a long chain of command which went back to the United Nations in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time a major got killed, a British major; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Corporal. [Interpretation] Do you know how that happened?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was caught between -- in cross-fire between the Serb side and the Bosnian government side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it actually correct that he was killed by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Difficult to say in the circumstances, but they had stayed too long reporting contact between the two sides. And as they were withdrawing and rounding the bend of a road, the vehicle was hit and he was killed. The report from the people on the ground believed that it was from the Serb side, but it was not deliberate firing, they said, from either side that killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you did not have any information to the effect that they were attacked by Muslims at Jabucko Sedlo, near the cemetery, near the Senokos facility?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the moment when a NATO airplane is attacking Serb positions, do Serbs, in your view, have the right to respond, to fire back?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right -- Serbs had no right in the first place to be in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, General. I like to say the following: If I ask you what day it is today and you say, "Five past 10.00," that is the correct time but it's not an answer to my question. So could you please tell me if a NATO airplane targets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I have to interrupt you here because you're criticising the witness for giving the answer he gave. You are supposed to ask about facts and not about theoretical abstract matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is not theoretical, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was: "When a NATO airplane is attacking Serb positions, do Serbs, in your view, have the right to respond?" That is an abstract, theoretical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you want to focus it on the event which was at the beginning of your testimony [sic], then you should be specific. And then of course the answer given by Mr. Rose is certainly relevant for your question. So since you criticise Mr. Rose for not answering your question, I'm inviting you to put questions about facts rather than about abstract matters and law. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, at a moment when a NATO airplane near Gorazde fires at a Serb target, does the Army of Republika Srpska have the right to fire back at this NATO aircraft?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is still not a concrete question. Are you -- the only thing you changed is that you said "at Gorazde," but still it is not focused on a matter of fact. The reason, Mr. Lukic, why I'm intervening is the following: In the answer the witness gave, he expressed clearly that circumstances, specific circumstances, of the individual case may be relevant for what is a right and what is not a right. So apart from whether we should ask the witness about the legal situation -- but even if you do so, the answer clearly indicates that the witness considers it impossible or very difficult to answer such a question without taking into consideration the specific circumstances of the case. And he's right that that is relevant. Therefore, you should put not a hypothetical case to the witness, but you can ask him about an event that, in your view, happened. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under the circumstances in which you asked for the Serb positions to be targeted around Gorazde, NATO is sending aircraft. The Serbs who are on the ground and who are being targeted by NATO aircraft, should they just be there as sitting ducks or can they respond by firing back, bearing in mind all the circumstances that you are aware of and in which this NATO attack took place.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an alternative action that could have been taken by the Serbs, and that was to stop firing on the town of Gorazde and withdraw their troops from immediate contact. That would have avoided NATO dropping bombs or firing missiles at the Serb positions that were engaged in breaching 824 and 836, the United Nations Security Council Resolutions, which I was bound to use all means possible to deter attacks against those safe areas. NATO was responding in -- to a situation that had been created by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, what NATO was responding to and what they did not wish to respond to. But I'll try once again to get an answer to this question. At the moment when this aircraft is flying over Serb positions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you've got an answer to the question. If you want to put a follow-up question, that's fine, but you've got an answer to your question. I do not accept that you are criticising this witness for not answering your questions where he did, but follow-up questions on the matter, fine, but then perhaps without the introduction outside to get an answer to my question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is the follow-up question, General - sorry if I'm being difficult: At the moment when the aircraft is already above the Serb positions, this is no longer a situation in which the Serbs can stop the attack; right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No consultations. Write a note, Mr. Mladic. No consultations; they should take place during the break. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. Sorry to interrupt you in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't seem to have any luck with this question. At the moment when the aircraft is above Serb positions, it had set out to hit its target. Would you agree with me that at that point in time there is no time left for the Serbs to stop the attack and to have the airplane return?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was very different [Realtime transcript read in error "difficult"] from the one you described. The NATO aircraft flew several times over the predicted targets and fired warning chaff delta, dropping chaff delta or making sonic booms to inform the Serb side that they were under threat of use of lethal force. The Serbs ignored these warnings. In the end, NATO was obliged to carry out a live attack. I don't think at that point the Serbs had the right to fire at the NATO aircraft, given the warnings they had received, but they were determined to continue with their combat operations, and that was not a right that they should have been accorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We shall move on. The person guiding the plane is a member of UNPROFOR. Would you agree with me that he, together with the pilot, makes up the team that is attacking a Serb target?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, on the translation here, it should be: "A. The situation was very different from the one you described."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for looking at the transcript as well. It's usually reviewed after the session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you ordered NATO air-strikes on the 10th of April, 1994, you did not know what the boundaries were of that safe area; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact delineation of the safe area was never all together clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know how many Serb civilians were detained in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited the installation and I believe there were 3- to 500 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You took part in the negotiations in which the Serbs asked for their dead; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that particular request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I seek clarification. The question was: Did you know how many Serb civilians were detained in Gorazde? Your answer was: "I visited the installation and I believe there were 3- to 500 people there." Did you intend or not intend to say that you do not know whether they are civilians or was it a confirmation of the 3- to 500 people being civilians detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, it was confirmation of the fact that I did not know whether they would have been civilians or former military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Former military or military at present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Military people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Muslims often tried to involve UNPROFOR in the conflict to have them on their side; that's what they did in this case too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what the intentions or indeed the capabilities of the Bosnian government forces were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to go back to your statement, to paragraph 74. You say the United Nations, that is somewhere towards the end of this paragraph. "During the cease-fire, the United Nations hoped a political settlement would be reached." The political settlement pertained to the percentage of territory that was supposed to be given to the two sides. Who was the first one to come up with the 51/49 percentage proposal?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no specific knowledge as to where that figure came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Gorazde the Muslim units were in town itself; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the position of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the period before the Serb offensive into Gorazde or after it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Before.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had UNMOs there. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did the UNMOs, or military observers, report? Were there any soldiers of the Bosnian Muslims in Gorazde, regardless of the lack of confidence you had in them? Or what about the JCOs? What did they report once they arrived in Gorazde? Were there any forces of the Bosnian Muslims there in town?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were definitely Bosnian government forces in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to UNPROFOR, in Gorazde as a safe area, was it permissible to have forces of either side in town?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, the safe areas were areas where there was to be no -- by agreement of all parties, there were to be no military forces or, indeed, combat. And this was a way of preserving the lives of the civilians who lived there. I guess all sides cheated on that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There weren't any safe areas where Serbs lived, so I don't see how Serbs could have cheated.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I added the word "combat," because of course the Serb side attacked into these areas when they were not supposed to. Indeed, they had agreed not to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it the position of UNPROFOR that the Serb forces should not allow Muslim -- should not attack Muslim forces that are within safe areas?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where the system broke down. There was a failure by the warring parties to stick to the agreement that had been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. In Gorazde there was a division of the Muslim army - are you aware of that - the 82nd Division of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained I had no specific knowledge of any deployments or capabilities, but the description of a "division" sounds a little bit extreme to me, knowing what a normal division would look like, a theoretical observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you accept that if this is stated in Muslim documentation, namely, that the 82nd Division was stationed within Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what UNPROFOR did during your time to demilitarise the area of Gorazde and whether anything was done at all?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the battalion had deployed to Gorazde, which took place after the events of the first two weeks of April, certainly the unit there would have persuaded the Bosnian government forces not to take active part in any further military operations. Disarmament was not part of our programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 08145; that's the 65 ter number. Could we please have that document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we're waiting for it, Mr. Lukic, I wondered whether I understood your line of questioning and what you would like to know, and therefore would you please comment if I would formulate the following question before Mr. Rose answers it. Because if it's a question you're not interested in, then we'll let it go. Mr. Rose, the continued presence of Bosnian government military in Gorazde, did that not create a situation in which it would be difficult to blame the Serbs for acting against this presence by military means, where they were not supposed to be within Gorazde? Is that a question which focuses very much on what you'd like to know? Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It made it very difficult to be critical of the Bosnian Serb side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- when they were responding to attacks against them from within the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "responding to attacks," but I do understand from you that their mere presence was already in violation of the rules that applied for this safe area. So could you also answer the question more specifically on how I put it to you, that is, not in response to military action, but in response to even the mere presence, a continued presence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the view at the time of the United Nations was that the Bosnian government forces had the right to maintain infantry units or their own military units wherever they chose on their sovereign territory, that as long as the units were not active and merely maintained themselves as a response to -- for attacks if ever that occurred, that would be the status quo acceptable to the UN. It was when these units attacked out from within the safe areas that it made it impossible to sustain the concept of the safe areas which was dependent on agreements by all parties and not to use those safe areas for combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I notice that there is a slight - I wouldn't say contradiction - but inconsistency between one of your previous answers, where you said they were supposed not to be there and not take any military action, which suggests that the mere presence was already a violation. But I now understand that just being there and remaining silent, to say so, and not to move was considered not to be in violation of the concept of the safe area of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a -- it was certainly a violation, sir, but it was one that was accepted, I think, tacitly by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say the violation was so innocent, more or less, that it would not justify any action taken against it, but this is an interpretation then of what are acceptable and not acceptable violations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was certainly the status quo that I inherited when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may have a follow-up question on that question. Mr. Rose, what was the responsibility of UNPROFOR in a situation where within a declared safe area one of the parties was present in violation of the rules of the game as established for the safe area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I tried to explain, sir, the United Nations were not in a position to forcibly disarm anybody. Pressure could be brought to bear politically through the media on elements who kept their weapons within the safe area, that is, the Bosnian government; and certainly the subject was raised a number of times by the United Nations with the Bosnian government. But each time the Bosnian government would reply, we have the right to maintain military forces where we choose to, say the next level of argument was: Well, they must not be active in that case and must only be there for -- in the form of ultimate self-defence. And that became the accepted status quo that I inherited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I -- my question didn't deal with the right to disarm any of the parties. I'm just asking the question: If, according to the establishment of a safe area, it is a violation to be merely present as a military force inside of the safe area. I'm saying what did that kind of presence evoke by way of responsibility on the part of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only political pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To disarm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To disarm or to get the army out of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to hand in their weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to me as if that was addressing what would have been the agreement regarding the establishment of a safe area. If I understand you -- unless I am missing something, if I understand you well, you are saying no military presence is allowed within a safe area. Is that a starting point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, the military on the Bosnian side were often civilians or militia who merely were issued with weapons; therefore, it was difficult to say who was formed military units and who were not. In most cases, they were not formed military units; they were civilians who had got weapons and had formed themselves into military units. The wish of the United Nations when the discussions took place establishing the safe areas was that with the agreements of all parties they would disarm, not move the militias or people out of the safe areas, but disarm, hand their weapons in, and that would then guarantee the sanctity of that safe area. Unfortunately, the Bosnian government side failed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you now say these were civilians who were armed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many of them were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the debate gets extended and I will end it at that point because we'll never stop now. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. It's time for a break. We've deprived you of some time for your questions. We'll take a break after the witness has left the courtroom and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Rose, you were familiar with the various agreements that had been concluded concerning Srebrenica and Zepa which expressly contained provisions stating that the forces of the Muslim or Bosnian army had to either leave Zepa or hand over all of their weapons to UNPROFOR; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there at the time the agreement was made, but that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us you inherited the situation on the ground, which is that UNPROFOR tolerated the existence of armed elements of the Muslim army within the protected areas. It pertained to both Srebrenica and Zepa, as well as Gorazde and Sarajevo and Tuzla and Bihac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please help us to understand your answer. It's only recorded "that's."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Contrary to such practice, the purpose of such protected areas was to protect civilians and not soldiers controlled by Alija Izetbegovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the reason for establishing the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're on the topic of Gorazde, could we please have in e-court 65 ter number 1845.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 8145.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see in item 3 that Mr. Karadzic assured you that the intention of the Serb side was not to take Gorazde, and in your testimony yesterday you told us that it was how you saw things too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later in the document, in item 7 which is on the next page in this version, Mr. Karadzic told you that he could not take a decision in that regard on his own but that he had to consult the Security Council, as translated, or rather he specified the names of Koljevic, Krajisnik, Plavsic, and the defence minister, as well as that of the interior. In this chain, or rather, body which was supposed to make that decision, Mr. Karadzic did not include General Mladic. Were you familiar with the way of how decisions were made regarding Gorazde and who participated in that decision-making process?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 8 of the same document we see that Mr. Karadzic insisted on at least four months -- actually, that his side insisted on a permanent cessation of hostilities which would be at least of six months' duration. That was in item 1 or (i). So this too tallies with what you told us yesterday, which is that the Serb side constantly favoured a permanent cessation of hostilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next I would kindly ask for document 1D550 in e-court. We need page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, it is your testimony of the 7th of October, 2010. We're interested in lines 2 to 4. On that occasion you stated that it had been discussed previously and that the status was different for the Bosnian government side than it was for the Bosnian Serb side. Yesterday you explained that the UN recognised only Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state and that at the time Republika Srpska was not recognised as such an entity. My question is this: Is it then correct that with regards to same obligations there was a difference in treatment between the two warring parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslim and the Serb side? Or rather, is it correct that when implementing undertaken obligations, the two sides were treated differently?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the two things are logically connected. The UN mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina was to act impartially in respect of its treatment of all three sides and that we were delivering humanitarian aid to those three sides. When it came to trying to negotiate or broker a peace, we equally treated the three sides equally as one would have to do as an impartial mediator. Whether we were neutral in the long-term as to what the outcome would have been is another matter all together, but it did not enter into the calculation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time did you know, although I'm aware of the fact that you are not a lawyer - as you have pointed out - and you actually said at page 7405 on the 6th of October, 2010, in the trial of President Karadzic: [In English] "I'm no expert on international law." [Interpretation] Still, I am inclined to ask the following: Did you at the time know what it meant that the three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina were all constituent?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Muslims actually usurped the power in Bosnia-Herzegovina, portraying themselves as the only legitimate representatives on behalf of the entire state?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a matter of fact it was the Christian population that made up the majority of the population, that is to say Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will briefly turn to Bihac next. In e-court we need 1D551 which is your testimony in the Karadzic case of the 8th October 2010. We need page 39 in e-court, lines 5 through 8. Perhaps the page is not correct. We need page 7539, which is five pages back, lines 5 through 8. You were asked about an offensive of the Muslim army from Bihac and a counter-offensive undertaken by the Serb army: [In English] "Thank you, General. But they could fully envisage what would happen if we would launch a counter-offensive. You would attack them with sharp words and us with sharp bombs; right?" And your answer was: "I suppose you could put it like that." [Interpretation] The thrust of my questions was in this vein when I asked you whether there was a different treatment according to the sides. There was a drastic difference, as a matter of fact, General, and we'll get to that. You could ask that NATO undertake action against the Muslim side, but you were openly told that NATO would not act against the Muslim element in Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told on one occasion that the -- when the Bosnian Serb army breached the ultimatum regarding the total exclusion zone on Mount Igman and I discussed with the air commander in Italy the prospects of calling in air-strikes against those elements because they were engaging with the French forces on the ground that this would not be accepted by NATO. That was the only occasion I can remember discussing specifically air-strikes against the Muslim Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you are trying to tell us that on other occasions you did not ask that NATO bomb Muslim forces because of operations they were carrying out?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not in our remit to do so unless they were in breach of a particular ultimatum, and that was the only occasion I remember them being in breach of a NATO ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So if they violated the agreements they had signed with UNPROFOR, such as the agreement on demilitarisation of Srebrenica or Zepa or Gorazde, the Muslims were in no danger that action would be taken against them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so. I think certain explanation may be required to that answer, and that is that the United Nations were not deployed to enforce any peace or to prevent combat between the warring parties by the use of military force; they were there purely in a peacekeeping role. And that, I think, puts in context the position I've just described of the United Nations with regards to attacks by one party or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We keep going back to the topic of the humanitarian part of UNPROFOR mandate, but, as it seems, UNPROFOR also asked NATO to bomb the Serb side, save for the one occasion we have discussed. And if one applies common sense to that, one realises that it is no humanitarian issue but a military one; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect. The UN only required -- requested air-strikes when convoys were being held up or when attacks were being made into the safe areas or when weapons were taken from weapon-collecting points. In each occasion these acts were carried out by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never asked that Muslim attacks be sanctioned, the attacks they carried out from inside the protected areas, thus provoking counter-attacks by the Serb side; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "sanctioned."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never asked NATO aircraft support, you never asked them to bomb Muslim positions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I step in here for one additional question in that respect. Sir, you told us earlier that there was one occasion when air-strikes asked against Bosnian Muslim forces and you said that this would not be accepted by NATO. Do you know the reason for this denial by NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't, sir. We didn't officially ask for air-strikes. I discussed it with the air commander who was based in Italy, and he said that they would never accept air-strikes against the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you don't know the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not given a reason, sir, although I had my suspicions because by then NATO had quite clearly taken sides in this war, which the United Nations had not done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And just before my question Mr. Lukic asked you: "You never asked NATO aircraft support, you never asked them to bomb Muslim positions." And you said: "We did not." Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the -- apart from the one incident that I described on Mount Igman when the Bosnian government forces were in breach of a NATO ultimatum, not to have military forces within that total exclusion zone, there was no other occasion which would have justified it. Our job was not to try and stop the combat by force of arms from either side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, is it correct that armed Muslim forces by attacking Serb positions and withdrawing to a town which was inside the protected areas actually placed civilians in danger?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next I would kindly ask for 65 ter 9033 to be placed in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, it is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska of the 18th of April, 1994. We see there that there were NATO aircraft attacks underway which had bombed and fired at Bosnian Serb positions in the area of Gorazde. Simultaneously, we see Muslim forces attacking the Nisici plateau. We'll take a look at another document about this. What knowledge did you have about the co-ordination of NATO air-strikes and the attacks of Muslim forces from the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such co-ordination. Each NATO attack was mounted in response to a Serb attack on the safe area. We did not co-ordinate in any way a response. And of course NATO air-strikes were only delivered after due warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Such warnings obviously reached the Muslim forces as well. Did you inform them about that? Were they aware when you warned the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge as to whether they were intercepting our messages to the Serb side, but there is no reason why we should have warned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 8966 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It has to do with paragraph 87 of your statement. That's not the right number. It's not what we need. Perhaps we can use the ERN number to locate the right document. 04394709. It is the B/C/S version. The English version has the same number. General, at the top of the page we see the following: "NATO air raids on the positions of the Herzegovina Corps have provided direct support to the Muslim forces, allowing them to mount a counterattack along all axes." Were you receiving reports that the Muslim armed elements used NATO air-strikes to carry out attacks on Serb sides?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a completely incorrect assessment by Colonel Masal who wrote this signal. NATO did not co-ordinate in any way its activities with the Bosnian government forces. If the government -- Bosnian government forces chose to use an air-strike to carry out military activity, that was their concern, not ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the source of your knowledge that NATO did not co-ordinate its actions with the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was I that was calling the NATO air-strikes and in no way was I co-ordinating those air-strikes, timing them, or any other form of co-ordination with the Bosnian government forces. They were being called down in direct response to actions by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether my question was phrased properly or interpreted properly. I'm not trying to say that you took part in that. What I'm saying is the following: What is your source of information to the effect that, or rather, did NATO co-ordinate its activity with the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since NATO only carried out air-strikes as a result of a request by me, that could not have been the case because I was not co-ordinating the air-strikes to conform to any activity by the Bosnian government forces. That is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At paragraph 85 you explained that at that point in time Serb tanks had left the area and went in the direction of Visegrad. Now that we're discussing the attack against Gorazde that continued. So after that it was only the infantry that was involved in these attacks. Is that what we can infer on the basis of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Tanks can turn around and come back and artillery can fire and mortars can fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just for the record you initially called for 8966, where apparently in view of the ERN number you then used you intended to call for 65 ter 8996, which by the way is P731.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now paragraph 89 of your statement. You say the following: "On the 12th of April, 1994, Gorazde was relatively quiet until the Bosnian Government army," the BH Army, "began to fire mortars and mounted infantry attacks at the Bosnian Serb army from within the safe area," of Gorazde. I assume that yet again you did not ask for NATO to bomb Muslim positions because of this action?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. It was not within our mandate so to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My next question would precisely be as follows: What was -- what was it that the Muslims were supposed to do for you to ask to have their side bombed too?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've given you the one example where they breached a NATO ultimatum and I called for air-strikes; that's the only occasion I can remember. If they chose to attack out from within a safe area, that did not, in our view, justify using air-strikes against them even if NATO would have responded, which they - as I now know - would not have done. We would have of course not left that unremarked. We would have raised that incident with President Izetbegovic, pointed out to him that he was hazarding the safety and the lives of his own people in Gorazde, and we would have used all possible pressures, other than military force, use of military force, to stop that kind of incident reoccurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So once again it would be the way Dr. Karadzic had put it, you would only target them with sharp words; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what he -- how he likes to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Tuzla, that's where the command and the units of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were; in Sarajevo, of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; in Gorazde, units of the 82nd Division of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; in Srebrenica, the command and units of the 28th Division of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and in Zepa, the command of the units of the Zepa Brigade; in Bihac, the command of the units of the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina: All the mentioned locations had been declared safe areas. From all of these places active combat was launched against Serb positions; isn't that right? Is that your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly happened on a number of occasions from some of those safe areas. I can't confirm whether it happened from all safe areas. I don't, for example, remember anything happening from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your mandate, did you ever propose a review of the position involved, namely, that these were safe areas?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The topic of safe areas was under constant discussion within the United Nations because there was a, as you pointed out, some contradiction here. On the one hand the state, the recognised state of Bosnia-Herzegovina had every right to station its forces, such as they were, wherever it chose; on the other hand, it had agreed to demilitarise these safe areas. The fact that it had chosen not to do so and had, as you pointed out, launched out a number of actions from these safe areas was a matter of deep regret to the United Nations. We took up the matter frequently with President Izetbegovic and the vice-president, Mr. Ganic, and we tried to point out that all they were doing was hazarding the lives of their civilians living in those areas and making it difficult to bring about peace. But as I equally pointed out, by then the Bosnian government side had determined that they would be more likely to regain their lost territories by war means than by the peace process. And so they were being unhelpful at that point to the United Nations peace effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have document 65 ter 08714 in e-court. It should be in this document, but I seem to be unable to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It has to do with paragraph 95 of your statement. However, the document was shown to you but you didn't really comment upon it. However, we can see from this document that the report says that it was Muslims that fired at NATO aircraft. Did you ever receive such information, namely, that Muslims had opened fire at NATO aircraft?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about the Gorazde incident, I received no such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This mainly has to do with the shelling of the town of Doboj in northern Bosnia that was shelled by the Muslim forces every day throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any knowledge of any firing on NATO aircraft in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please give me a moment. We'll have to move on. I cannot find it now so we'll have to go back. As for humanitarian aid - and you say that that is what UNPROFOR was primarily in charge of - is it correct that anywhere in the world it is soldiers who first receive humanitarian aid and it is only afterwards that all others do? Was that the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no specific evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- could we first -- these are -- a question starts with a general observation. I think it would be fair that we first ask whether you do agree with this general observation that humanitarian aid is always everywhere in the world received first by the military and only then by those for whom it is intended. Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the second question, whether this happened here as well, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall any specific incidents where we discovered United Nations' supplies in the front line, but I think it was certainly happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you then that all the humanitarian aid that came in was first given to the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. The way the system worked is we would hand it over at a distribution point to local representatives from the community, who very often would then subsequently hand it on to the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. To that extent, the humanitarian aid was supporting the fitness of the military primarily; is that -- that is the consequence of your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's an inevitable consequence of a humanitarian aid programme, but the alternative is worse in the view of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I perhaps ask one follow-up question. Were you referring to situations of armed conflict or were you talking in general about humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Situations of armed conflict, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In armed conflict. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask for 65 ter number 8714. Could we please have that in e-court. We need the bottom of the page in B/C/S, the beginning. The very bottom of the page. I do apologise. And page 2 in English. It's quite illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That question of mine is based on this document. It says at 1640 hours an area -- in the area of Gorazde --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find this reference and it's being read out too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you try to find for us what you're reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 8189 is the 65 ter number that I actually need. We see it at the bottom of the page of this document and it's on page 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you tell us is this document 8714 or 8189?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 8189, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And to what part of the page must we look in the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's just below the -- if you are referring to the paragraph which mentions 1640 hours, it would be the paragraph just below the middle of the page "in the area of responsibility" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you see this report where it says that an aircraft had been hit in the area of Gorazde and that it was fired at from Muslim-held territory and it crashed on Mount Jahorina? Do you see that it's in the document? Do you believe that Serbs would be gloating if they had downed the aircraft? Do you think that that's what they would be doing rather than saying it's the other side that downed it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say without commenting on the Serbs or the Muslim position is that the pilot who I had spoken to and NATO were quite sure that the aircraft was -- if it's the Harrier aircraft we're referring to - was shot down by Serb ground-to-air missiles. They are having taken that view because they saw previous missiles fired at them but missing; on this occasion, it hit. So I think that report is completely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that the only aircraft that had been shot down in the area of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this report in paragraph 4 - so we need the next page in English now and in B/C/S - we probably have to go further ahead in English, one page up. Let's see number 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm also looking at the clock. It's approximately time. So perhaps you reorganise your sources and then we can more efficiently proceed. But before we take a break, I'd like to ask one additional question on a matter which is still puzzling me, that is, the military receiving or benefitting first from humanitarian aid. You said this is considered -- the other option would even consider to be worse. Now, I've been thinking about what the other option would be, that would be that you would not provide humanitarian aid at all. And do I then understand that the risk that there are even not any leftovers for the civilian population would be the worst situation. Is that how I have to understand it or ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, the quantity of aid being delivered was sufficient for 2.7 million refugees who were dependent on that aid in Bosnia-Herzegovina. An element of that aid certainly would have gone to the soldiers on the front line, many of whom of course were civilians anyway but merely taking up their position on rotation in the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was impossible therefore to say that no aid went to the front line, and typically in an environment like that the soldiers would be fed first and then the remainder of the aid would go to the civilian population. And I think that was probably the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But not to have delivered aid would have been unacceptable to the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now I better understand the worse alternative as you called it. We take a break and we resume at a quarter past 12.00, but first could the witness leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I use the time meanwhile, Mr. Lukic, but I'm also addressing you -- I'm also addressing the Prosecution, Ms. Bibles. I rephrased or at least I phrased a question, Mr. Lukic, in a way because I thought that that is the question you'd like to seek an answer to. Now, at the same time in that question - and I followed you there, rightly or not - there was a suggestion that the permanent presence of military in the safe area of Gorazde was prohibited. Now, the Chamber is a bit confused now and then about what is the legal instrument by which some behaviour or activity is prohibited. For example, do the Security Council Resolutions - you might think of 824 and 836 - do they impose an obligation to withdraw troops, of whatever kind, from all places near the safe areas? Or is it on the basis of an agreement between the parties? And whenever you ask questions like: Why didn't you respond with force, air-strikes? Then of course the question arises: What were the limits of the use of force? What were the conditions? Et cetera, et cetera. And in order to avoid any confusion in that respect, the Chamber would very much like to receive from the parties the texts which are determining the -- the -- at the various moments in time were determining conditions, definition of safe areas, et cetera, so that we are better able to understand the testimony and sometimes the questions that are put to witnesses. Mr. Rose, I addressed the parties when you came in. We'll now proceed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with your cross-examination. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see in item 4 - and that's where we left off, General - it is the Main Staff of the VRS document of the 16th of April, 1994. In item 4 we have a description of the situation with regards to the air-space. It reads: "The enemy continued with reconnaissance activities, the training of plane crews and exercising power in Republika Srpska air-space. The focal point of the NATO Air Force runs was in the areas of Sarajevo - Gorazde, Kupres - Bugojno, Tuzla - Brcko - Doboj, Banja Luka - Gradiska and occasionally Mostar - Konjic and Petrovac - Bihac. A total of 108 enemy formations have been detected and observed, out of which five were in the territory of Croatia." It is obvious that at that point in time Serbs considered NATO airplanes enemy airplanes, as we can see from this document. Perhaps you can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see from the document that Serbs considered NATO airplanes enemy airplanes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't comment on the Serbs' attitude towards NATO, but I could understand if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The sorties of such planes, as we can see here there were 108 enemy formations. Well, what was the goal of those flights? Were they of humanitarian nature? Military nature? Reconnaissance? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I disagree with the use of the word "enemy." NATO were there to enforce the no-fly zone. They were there to provide close-air defence for the United Nations peacekeepers on the ground. And they were there to enforce the passage of convoys, to deter attacks against safe areas, which I think is the reading of 824, et cetera. It was not there to wage war against any side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whether they were waging war or not, NATO airplanes had already bombed Serb positions and only Serb positions, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already identified that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it justified in your view from a military standpoint?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not have called in air-strikes if I hadn't felt they were justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it justified from a military standpoint that the Serbs were preparing themselves to be targeted by NATO airplanes again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are referring to "from a military standpoint." I think if we understand the testimony of this witness well, the use of force, military force, was ruled by - and this comes back to the issue I raised before the witness came in after the break - was ruled by the mandate of those who were tasked with supervising and by the United Nations Security Council to perform their jobs; and to the extent allowed by that, to call for support by those who had airplanes available. And now -- and then to put "from a military point of view," which very much sounds as if it was just an ordinary combat situation. So I would like you to clearly take into consideration the testimony of the witness on the situation which existed and then to explore what you would like to know about what was justified and what was not justified on the basis of the mandate, on the basis of who decided on it, who then called for it. And then as a part of that, perhaps also if you want to include that matters like: Was it an air-strike against an individual soldier somewhere? That is then the last portion of a whole and a complex series of events and considerations and you cannot just simplify the situation and say: From a military point of view was it justified? You need to address all the various aspects of that question because otherwise it wouldn't assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will try to abide by your instructions, although I am of the opinion that the area I have been exploring is not as broad. I'm simply trying to establish the fact that the Serbs considered that NATO was the enemy at the time. I wanted to establish that their view was justified and what the consequences were as regards the movement of convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just justify it or not requires to look at it in such detail and what the attitude of the Serbs was, the witness has several times said "I do not know." What you can ask him is under what legal or military regime the actions were taken as they were taken and then to explore them in such a way that it enables the Chamber to form its judgement on what was justified or what was not justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, I do not believe that a Serb soldier in the field was interested in the legal standpoint --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I didn't invite you -- I mean, I gave you my guidance. Then you re-opened more or less a debate. Then I gave you again my guidance. And now to do it for a third time, there's no need to do that. Just proceed and elicit the evidence from the witness which you consider to be relevant with my guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here that the plane flights occurred at the time not only in the crisis areas, such as Gorazde, Sarajevo, we see that they also flew over Kupres, Bugojno, Tuzla, Brcko, Doboj, Banja Luka, Gradiska. In those areas, if you know, why were there NATO flights there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to ask NATO that question. NATO was embarked, as I've already stated, on a -- enforcing a no-fly zone and it was in support of that mission or in support of the United Nations peacekeepers on the ground that they were in the air at all. So it would have been one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any case, these NATO planes were not there for humanitarian reasons, were they? They were not delivering humanitarian aid? That was the thrust of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the question has been answered. The witness has said what it was and that had got nothing to do with humanitarian aid. It was to ensure the no-fly zone or to give the necessary report to what happened on the ground, I take it, with the agreement and the approval of all relevant authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I could add one more thing, sir, and that is that I think early in the spring of 1994 there was still a programme of air-dropping humanitarian aid to a number of the enclaves, such as Maglaj, although that was terminated because we were able to deliver aid by land after that. So there was some active air-dropping of humanitarian aid by NATO in the early part of that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in mid-April 1994 there were air-drops of humanitarian aid still in place?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they had terminated possibly by mid -- that year. I don't know the exact date. But you should also remember that a lot of the air landed aid to Sarajevo airport came through NATO as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have in e-court P732, which is a document you have commented upon yesterday during your examination-in-chief. It is related to paragraph 96 of your statement. We see that it is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where it is stated that pursuant to an oral order of the president of Republika Srpska the following is being ordered. In the last paragraph which you commented upon it is stated as follows: "Immediately take measures to intensify security and control over the members of UNPROFOR and international humanitarian organisations. In case of massive air attack against units and facilities of the RS, the said must be immediately disarmed, arrested, and the weaponry and combat equipment confiscated and used for anti-aircraft combat."
