Your interpretation yesterday at transcript page 6857 in this trial, lines 3 through 15, was that you understood it to mean that the manpower should be used for anti-aircraft combat by exposing them to NATO bombardment. In B/C/S and in the English version as far as I can see, if we look at the translation and the semantics, one would not conclude that because it says the weaponry and combat equipment should be confiscated and used for anti-aircraft combat. Would you agree that based on this document one cannot conclude anything other than what we can read in it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I stand corrected in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move to paragraph 97 of your statement. We also need document 8734. It is a 65 ter document. On page 2 -- well, we can see that it is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska dated the 20th of April, 1994. On page 2 in the B/C/S, which is also page 2 in the English, the part describing the situation in the corps begins. We are interested in sub-item (c), we find it on page 3 in the English, whereas in the B/C/S it's still on the same page. We see again -- well, it reads as follows: "The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps: The 1st rpbr, as part of the 'Zvijezda 94' operation, is engaged in active operations in the direction of Orahovica and Datelj. The other units of the Corps are at full-scale combat-readiness in order to prevent any surprises by Muslims and UNPROFOR." We see again that the Serb side saw Muslims and UNPROFOR as one side to the conflict. I wanted to ask you this: At the time, were the humanitarian aid convoys stopped? Was there a cessation of their movement at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you expect such a cessation in the movement of convoys following your order for NATO to carry out air-strikes on Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would you allow me to go back to one of your previous questions, that was about the interpretation of the document whether it said that the weaponry and the combat equipment confiscated from UNPROFOR members and international humanitarian organisations to be used for anti-aircraft combat, was the weaponry and the equipment of UNPROFOR which you could confiscate, would that be -- could that be militarily -- properly be used in anti-aircraft combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm -- not really. So I know it was small arms we carried and the chances of hitting a fast-moving jet were minute. When I read that statement the first time, I was referring to the fact that on a number of occasions UN personnel were definitely placed by potential NATO targets in order to protect them. And I was assuming that both weapons and personnel were being referred to by that last bit of the statement, but I'm much relieved to hear that it was only the weapons that they thought were going to be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me read it then again the line to you. Perhaps we could have it on the screen again. This was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P732, paragraph 4, page 1 in English. And I slowly read it again, "In case there is a massive" -- I beg your pardon, it's not on the screen yet. Yes, it's at the bottom of this page. I start halfway: "In case there is a massive air attack on units and facilities of the RS, the said must be immediately disarmed," and that's a reference to UNPROFOR, members of UNPROFOR, international humanitarian organisations, "arrested and the weaponry and combat equipment confiscated and used for the anti-aircraft combat." Now, apparently we are at this moment interpreting a text. I'm not a native English-speaking person, but I wondered whether the word "used" here where there's no specific reference to any of the previous portions of what had to be done, that is, persons to be disarmed and arrested, weaponry and equipment to be confiscated and used, whether there's any -- in terms of language, whether there's any ambiguity in what "used" would refer to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there is, sir. I think you could read that statement as the UN must be immediately disarmed, arrested, and weaponry -- it's disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be still there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UN must be immediately disarmed, arrested, and the weaponry and combat equipment confiscated and used could refer to both the weaponry and the personnel if you wanted to read it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it's not unambiguous in the English version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] No. So that's why I in my first statement yesterday assumed that they were also referring to the UN personnel being used as well as the equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I'm relieved to be corrected by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you're corrected or whether the ambiguity is there and not resolved, we might have to go back to the original language because that's the language the author used and perhaps ask whether a similar ambiguity does exist in the B/C/S version of this document. That would be the best way to proceed. Mr. Lukic, perhaps we could find a way to see whether a similar ambiguity is found in the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not a translator, but according to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said let's ask for --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there is -- according to me there is not any ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could be. Then we should seek a better translation so as not to be confused. Could -- it's a document you presented, Ms. Bibles. Could you perhaps briefly seek from the CLSS a short memo on whether the ambiguity which is by a native-speaking person but apparently also by me has been noted, whether a similar ambiguity exists in the original language.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will do that immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of any linguistic problems, although I believe there are none, I wanted to go back to these combat assets. The weapons and combat equipment were to be seized and used for anti-aircraft combat. Combat equipment in this case would also include communications equipment that some of the UNPROFOR members had with them in order to guide planes; is it not correct? Did some UNPROFOR members have such combat equipment used to communicate with NATO airplanes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could that be used in, for instance, alarming the troops or guiding them to a wrong target?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please explain why not.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the pilots of the aircraft would have detected immediately that they were being improperly used by other parties. They would not have had the codes and they wouldn't have had the language to be able to direct aircraft wrongly, even if the Serbs had tried so to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By seizing such equipment, would precise guidance and targeting have been prevented?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I will leave this topic now. Where was I before I went back to this topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were with a different document. That's what I remember, Mr. Lukic. I caused the disturbance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 99 of your statement, General. There you discuss the 23rd of April, 1994. You say that an agreement was reached following the NATO ultimatum and UN Resolution 913: "The agreement included an immediate cease-fire in and around Gorazde and the creation of a 3-kilometre exclusion zone from which the Bosnian Serb sources would withdraw, as well as the creation of a 20-kilometre heavy weapons exclusion zone, medical evacuation for the wounded, and freedom of movement for UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations." By virtue of this agreement, were any obligations placed upon the Muslim side, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think there were other than they should desist from using the safe areas - which was a general point we continually made to them - for military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So they did not have to disarm; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not part of the agreement, as far as I can remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, 100, which is a continuation, if you will, but in general terms you say: "From my experiences and observations of the events surrounding the BSA's attempted take-over of Gorazde in April 1994, I am of the view that had the take-over succeeded, the Bosnian Serbs would have placed further pressure on the Bosnian government to accept a global cessation of hostilities and thereby cement the territorial gains of the Bosnian Serb army." Can we say that the activities of UNPROFOR and NATO prevented precisely this from happening?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the fact that they had been bombed, the Serbs, both in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Yugoslavia, had sanctions imposed upon them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Muslims constantly provoked conflicts from within the safe areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were certainly in the habit of doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Western media at the time were partial and they reported only to the advantage of the Muslim side, and in that way they turned the Western public opinion against the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that probably is in -- largely the case, although there were a number of honest, hard-working reporters who tried to give a balanced point of view; but the general impression internationally was as you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The leaders of NATO and the politicians from these states were also on the side of the Bosnian Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no evidence to say that was the case, but my belief certainly in retrospect is that sometime during 1994 the NATO led by the Americans decided to breach their own United Nations Security Council Resolutions regarding the arms embargo and started to train and equip the Muslims and the Croats. And that, therefore, inevitably placed NATO on one side and the Serbs on the other, leaving the United Nations trying to hold the two sides from the middle. It certainly made the peacekeeping mission almost impossible to proceed with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that peace plans were always formulated so as to go against the interest of the Serbs and also to improve the position of the Muslims in the field?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the case. I think every effort, honest effort was made by the peace-brokers such as Dr. Owen, Mr. Stoltenberg, Mr. Vance, to try and reach a fair but enduring peace. And certainly the figure as I have described oscillated between 51 per cent for the Serbs and 49 per cents for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Sorry, Mr. Rose. You did say 51 per cent for the Serbs and 49 per cent for the Serbs. Would you like to correct one of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be 49 per cent for the Bosnian state in some iterations of the agreement, whereas the Serbs were looking for 51 per cent for themselves. So from their negotiating point of view they wished to have 51 per cent plus a number of important areas. But the offer was never rarely more than 49 per cent for them by the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I did not phrase the question properly, but this is what I wanted to ask. The peace plans that were offered always offered less to the Serbs compared to what they held in the field then in terms of the percentage of the territory they had in their hands. And then on the other hand they always offered more to the Muslims that they had actually held in their hands at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was always the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 1D548 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, this is your testimony from the Karadzic case on the 5th of October, 2010. I'm going to read out a section first and then I'm going to put a question to you. We need page 9 in e-court and it should be 7249 of the transcript, lines 8 through 15. Could we see that, please. You are talking about a turning point here in 1994 when the balance of power shifted, and this is the question: "Did this transformation, or the culminating point, as you have described it, have any relationship to the positions taken at international peace negotiations? "A. It most certainly did, because, of course, the Bosnian federation became more encouraged in their strategy of not signing up to any peace accord which they felt was unjust and rewarded the aggressor, and, of course, they had the support of NATO, and the Americans in particular, in that position." This is precisely in keeping with what you said to us a moment ago at this trial; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is my view and remains my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- could I -- still in relation to this, the matter of the percentages and the negotiations about that have been dealt with earlier today, Mr. Lukic, and I made a note with one of your questions. The witness - I'm talking about page 7, line 7 and following - testified that he was aware that there was a discussion about 49/51 per cent, but he explained that the situation was far more complicated because of the specific wishes in relation to that. Your next question then was: "As you have said yourself, on one side there were the Muslims and Western powers, and on the other side the Serbs, when it comes to the percentage negotiations." That was your question. And the answer was: "I guess that that was probably the situation." Now, I wondered when you put that question what exactly it meant and what it meant what the witness told us. Did you mean to say that they were siding with the Muslims as a general observation, which of course would have its effect as well during these negotiations? Or was it that the international community shared the Muslim views that the Serb proposals in terms of 49/51 per cent were unreasonable, and therefore at that point not in general about division of territory but specifically in relation to what was finally the discussion, which side of the 50 per cent, that they shared the views of the Muslims there? So I'm -- it was presented more or less as on the one side the Muslims and the international community, the other side the Serbs, whether that was the overall situation when it came to division of territory or whether it was specifically on the 49/51 per cent that the international community sided with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm guessing here, sir, because obviously I was not party to these various discussions and negotiations. The Contact Group, for example, excluded the UN for that -- from their discussions, but my general view is that the international community wished to bring about an enduring and a just peace, which meant going along roughly the lines of 49 per cent for the Serbs and 51 per cent for the Bosnian government. I'm sure the Bosnian government wished to have a great deal more than that, but that was the general international view that that was the fair and enduring settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, siding with the Muslims in acceptance of what the international community considered here to be a reasonable --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- proposal and not going any further .

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because your answer was: "I guess that was probably the situation ..." It needs -- we needed to fully understand what the situation was which was depicted in the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I guess so because I use the word "I guess," because of course I wasn't party to those discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to move on to more specific matters after having dealt with these general matters. And now let us look at paragraph 102 of your statement. You say: "The Bosnian Serbs had indeed launched a significant attack on Gorazde in which civilians were killed and injured and had been unconcerned about the plight of civilians caught up in the fighting. They had undoubtedly directed artillery fire and tank fire at the Bosnian army in the town ..." General, you said earlier on that you knew that in Gorazde there were quite a few combatants but they were hardly discernible from civilians. There were people in civilian clothing who carried a rifle nevertheless or were for a while members of a particular unit and then they would be at home. So this is my question: Would you agree with me that it was extremely difficult in that fighting to distinguish between civilians and soldiers in the area of Gorazde among the Muslim population, that is?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Difficult to be specific because if the Bosnian government forces were fighting outside of the town, as they were, across the bridge on the other side of the river, then it would have been easy to identify them as soldiers. If they were fighting in and around the edges of the town, then it may have been less easy to distinguish them. But of course if someone is carrying a rifle or firing it or some other weapon then you can identify them anyway as soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that fighting in Gorazde took place from one house to the other, that the fighting had actually spilled over into the town itself, although on the edges?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it crossed over the bridge into the main part of the town. The villages --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the other side of the town were being --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Villages, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, can I make a plea to terminate at this point. I think I probably drunk too much coffee during the lunch break, the previous break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take an early break. We'll resume then at 1.30 and we'll then continue until quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you first follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I had intended to raise this at a time when there was free court time, but given your question at the beginning of the session I think it's relevant to bring it up now. The Prosecution was going to seek an exception to the guidance and request permission to file a bar table motion with relevant UN documents. We thought that it would be beneficial for the Chamber to have those at this stage of the trial rather than to wait until the end of the case, and we are in the process of preparing such a bar table motion. But I may ask for the Chamber to consider whether we would be allowed to file such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course the Chamber asked this morning for at least some documents. What I would suggest is that if you make such a filing, that you would make it a combined filing and that the Defence adds to the series of documents you consider to be relevant those they consider to be relevant, perhaps including some agreements between the parties as well. So this kind of, if I could say, legal stuff. Mr. Lukic, would you be willing to consider that together with Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. You know we co-operate well with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no doubt about that. I confidently ask you. We -- so, Mr. Groome shall therefore proceed, perhaps co-operating with Mr. Lukic, and we now take the break, resuming at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, are you all right? Can we go on now? Now I would briefly like to deal with paragraphs 105 and 106 from your statement, that is, and in connection with that I would kindly ask for 65 ter 8146 in e-court. We see the document. It's a fax. It has to do with the agreement on Gorazde, and the fax is dated the 21st of May, 1994. On the second page of this document, which we need to see on the screen now, we see the agreement on demilitarisation -- actually, the agreement on the demilitarisation of the 3 kilometre total exclusion zone east of the Drina River. We see when it will enter into force. We see that in paragraph 1. We see when the cease-fire will start. And then in paragraph, 3 it says: "The BiH commander commits himself to not undertake any offensive action. The only armed personnel in the shaded area on the attached map will be those of UNPROFOR." On page 4 of this document that we need to see in e-court now we can see this map, so that the General can remember what all of this is actually about. The shaded area is actually Gorazde on the right bank of the Drina River; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did that, or rather, do you remember whether members of UNPROFOR entered that zone?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. And if you're referring to the shaded zone, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] Did the parties abide by this agreement? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to move to paragraph 112 of your statement -- actually, this is an explanation of document 65 ter 8148, so could that please be displayed in e-court. You are familiar with the form of document that we see here, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here that Mr. Akashi is writing to Mr. Annan at the UN on the 4th of June, 1994. We will need page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm still seeking some clarification of -- we don't have to move back in documents to the earlier one. Your question was whether the parties abided to this agreement which was signed by General Milovanovic and General Rose. In 106 we see that the witness gives us evidence that Ganic refused to sign any agreement. Your next questions were about whether the parties -- now, that's ambiguous language again, parties, parties to the conflict? And abide to an agreement, where we learn from the evidence that the Bosnians apparently did not want to sign that. So was there any agreement? Were there any parties to an agreement? Or were there just the warring parties? I'm a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was asking about Gorazde, and in 106 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it's telling about sniping in Sarajevo

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me see. 106, yes anti-sniping agreement -- yes. Now, I may have been confused because I didn't see the signature of the Bosnian government. I think I saw two signatures on the copy you showed to us, therefore I not sufficiently carefully read 106 dealing with a totally different matter. Yes, Judge Moloto points at that 106 says "any agreement," whether that's limited to anti-sniping agreements or to other agreements and whether it was just a refusal to sign or also to refuse to commit yourself to it, which is not exactly the same, you can orally agree with something and then nevertheless refuse to sign. It's unclear. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- seek clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, sorry, from the copy that we have I cannot even tell whether it had been signed or not. So can we please have -- just a moment, please. 8146 on our screens again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have both pages 2 and 3 because they were signed both in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see the same blot, if you will, by General Delic's name both in English and in Serbian, but perhaps it was signed using some pencil or pen that faded in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did sign it at that time, Delic, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you considered UNPROFOR to be a witness to this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- agreement between the parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please proceed. Yes, it's not visible. I do agree that if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can see that the next page [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, page 3 is better --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now we're dealing with document 8148, the fax that was sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan. And in this document we need page 2 since we need paragraphs 6 and 7. We see here that paragraphs 6 and 7 speak of armed civilians who are refusing to withdraw from the right bank of the Drina River, roughly that shaded area that we saw a moment ago. In paragraph 7 Mr. Akashi says that Dr. Karadzic stated that these are remaining elements of demobilised soldiers who were not under control and that some of them were not following General Mladic's orders. As Mr. Akashi says, he, however, telephoned his people in Pale and issued orders for the immediate withdrawal of these elements. General, did you know that in part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska there were armed elements that were not under General Mladic's command and control? Had you heard of -- have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not. Our view was quite specific that these soldiers hadn't moved out as ordered. Whether that was a game play on the part of the Bosnian Serbs or not we don't know. And when we challenged them, you can see an account of the reply we had from Mr. Karadzic. But the situation was finally resolved and all elements, whether they were so-called policemen, armed civilians, or whoever, were finally moved from that 3-kilometre zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning paragraph 125 of your statement, with regards to that paragraph we also need document 8149. We need paragraph 2. It's a fax message. It concerns a meeting with General Mladic on the 21st of July, 1994. In item 2 it is stated that you, General Rose, protested since in air-space near Sarajevo airport in the previous 24 hours, including two that morning, fire was opened at UN planes. You asked that an immediate investigation be made and action taken as appropriate. We see in brackets that you were informed ten minutes later by General Galic that the shooting came from a particular building on the Bosnian Muslim side of the confrontation line in Sarajevo. This information is still unconfirmed. General, was it finally established who opened fire at the planes on those three occasions, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was never established clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it was standard practice to lay the blame on the Serbs first and then it was up to them to disprove that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that was the case at all. We merely -- I tried to identify in difficult circumstances where the fire had come from and would then go to that respective party to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let me ask you something about paragraph 127 of your statement. There you discuss the tunnel. Obviously UNPROFOR was aware of it as was also testified to by some other UNPROFOR members. You say there the following: "All the supplies that were going through the tunnel under the airfield came down through Mount Igman - this route was important to the UN aid convoys, as well as to the racketeering being conducted by the warring factions." During your stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina did anyone acquaint you with the initial document by virtue of which the Serbs handed over the control of the airport to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did see the original agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P334 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic kindly speak into the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreters invite you to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, on the screen we have the agreement on the re-opening of Sarajevo airport for humanitarian purposes. We see immediately that it is 1992. We're interested in paragraphs 4 and 6 which is on the next page. General, in item 4 we see that UNPROFOR took upon itself to control all incoming personnel, aid, cargo, and other items entering the airport, so as to ensure that no war time materials are imported and that the airport's opening is not otherwise abused in any way. Of course the issue of the tunnel somewhat complicates matters. But let me ask you this: The French soldiers who were at the airport, did they inform you about the existence of the tunnel? And did they tell you that they were aware of its existence? Did they inform you that they actually took part in expanding the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I ever discussed the existence of the tunnel with the French.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that score, let me ask you the following: The system of reporting within UNPROFOR, did it go towards the governments and intelligence services of the respective countries first and did various elements of UNPROFOR have an opportunity or an option not to inform other elements of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with regards to the latter part of your statement, of course that was the case. There was always a national position taken and any instructions given by UNPROFOR to the troop-contributing nations would always have to be ratified by their governments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know whether I fully understand the link between question and answer. Was it your question, Mr. Lukic, whether before reporting to the UNPROFOR superiors that the information was first submitted to the national governments of the relevant UNPROFOR person or unit resulting perhaps in information not reaching the UNPROFOR higher level by being stuck through the local -- through the national governments of the UNPROFOR units? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was exactly my point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't think that the -- I don't know whether the answer really responds to that. Could you expand on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I would agree that each of the troop-contributing nations had their own national policy with regards to the mission and they had their own reporting chains back to their governments. Now, what went up and down those reporting chains, I of course have got no knowledge of. I do believe that with regards to the French they gave me all the necessary information I needed to be able to administer the mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may have been filtered to the sense that some information which was stopped by the French government never reached you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That could well have been the case and that would have been so of all the troop-contributing nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning the airport you do not recall the agreement. Can you tell us what governed your actions concerning the airport? Were you simply briefed and continued with what you had inherited?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The importance of the airport was to be -- enable humanitarian aid to be flown in and people, casevac cases, et cetera, to be flown out. What was happening on the perimeters or underneath were signs that I may have been -- heard of in terms of rumour, but certainly never had confirmed during my time there. And you should also understand that it was, I guess, suited everybody that supplies and aid should be coming in to Sarajevo by -- no matter by what means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 128 of your statement you say that you learned that Dr. Karadzic, save for being stubborn, he also stated that there was smuggling of weapons into Sarajevo as part of the commercial traffic and that the failure of Bosnians to sign up to the anti-sniping agreement and prison exchange programme was the situation in place. You conclude by saying that finally the cease-fire agreement was sabotaging the cease-fire agreement signed in Geneva. A reference is made to a document and it reads that for security reasons you felt compelled to close down the airport. In your previous answer you said that it was in everybody's interest to see goods coming into Sarajevo through the tunnel. Let me ask you this: Do you allow for the possibility that through the tunnel, especially at night, weapons were being brought in, military equipment, and troops into Sarajevo as well as troops leaving Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that was a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this paragraph we have a reference to 60.000 civilians coming into or leaving Sarajevo. It all took place as of the opening of the airport routes in March 1994. It is stated that 60.000 civilians left. How do you know -- actually, if you know, how was the entry and exit of civilians and/or soldiers in Sarajevo controlled? And do you know whether any such control existed in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the convoys going in and out of Sarajevo were administered by the UNHCR, United Nations Commission for Refugees. That figure would have come from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You believed that the civilians coming into or leaving Sarajevo were onboard UNPROFOR trucks or did they leave on foot? It is unclear to me. These 7.000 trucks, did they transport goods only - because obviously we're discussing delivery of humanitarian aid - or the passage of people? Do you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly there were buses running in and out of Sarajevo for many of those months we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 129, the last sentence: "The Bosnian Serbs realised they were being seen as aggressors, and thought BH command was taking sides." Did UNPROFOR see the Serbs as aggressors; and if so, please tell us what the definition of "aggressor" was under UNPROFOR terms. What is an aggression?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN were acting impartially as mediators and had no position to take on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, who was it then that viewed the Serbs as aggressors? Because obviously the Serbs realised they were being seen as aggressors. Who believed them to be the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the Bosnian government referred to them almost universally as the aggressors, and that was often reflected in the propaganda put out by the media who sided with the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that in the fall of 1994 the Serbs blocked the airport, you mention a number of reasons: One was that the pressure be brought upon the Muslim side so as to force them to accept the peace conditions; under two, that the Muslims be forced into signing an anti-sniping agreement; three, that Sarajevo be demilitarised. Although it is partially self-explanatory, I still need to ask you the following: The Muslims obviously didn't want any of the three conditions - correct? - they wouldn't accept any peace conditions; they wouldn't sign an anti-sniping agreement; and they did not consent to Sarajevo being demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th of August they signed an anti-sniping agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the agreement implemented following its signing?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was implemented and it held good for a number of weeks, but it in the end declined on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have 1D548 in e-court. It is your testimony of the 5th of October, 2010, General. First we'd like to see page 16 in e-court. The very bottom of page 16. We need page 7256 which is page 16 in e-court. Reference is made to the same paragraphs we have mentioned today in your statement: [In English] " ... in your written evidence, at paragraphs 127 to 129, you referred to an event somewhat earlier than that, the closure of the airport to commercial convoys using the road down Mount Igman ..." [Interpretation] On the next page starting with line 2 there is a question: [In English] "Are you able to put this in context for us, this event?" And then your answer follows: "I think this was happening for two reasons: 1, that the pressure, again, not only strategically, needed to be brought to bear on the Bosnian government side to adopt their peace terms; but also to try and get them to sign up to the anti-sniper agreement; they also had a desire to have Sarajevo demilitarised. And I think they were" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. -- you were reading and that takes more time to translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "And I think they were the three areas which caused them to shut down the routes, because they could see that people now in Sarajevo on the Bosnian Muslim side were living far better than the people on the Bosnian Serb side ..." [Interpretation] General, can we conclude on the basis of that that humanitarian aid improved the situation in the Muslim part of Sarajevo to the extent that people in that part of Sarajevo lived much better than the people in the Serb-held part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a consequence of the opening of the routes rather than the delivery of humanitarian aid at that point, but certainly the end result was that the Serbs living in Golubovica [phoen] were not as well off as many of the people living in the rest of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Despite that, the Western powers and NATO kept insisting upon improving the living conditions of only the Muslim population in Bosnia, and Sarajevo in particular; is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true at all. The United Nations were impartial in their view as to what aid was required to the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and indeed it was the World Health Organisation that made assessments for the tonnages to be delivered to each of the three populations living there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's one question, please put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I apologise, I wasn't asking about UNPROFOR. I was inquiring about the insistence of NATO and Western powers to improve the living conditions of only the Muslim part of the population. I exclude UNPROFOR from that. The Western powers insist on improving the living conditions of only the Muslim part of population in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I completely disagree with that judgement and assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we adjourn for the day, could you give us an indication as where we stand in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I promise to finish tomorrow in the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have more but I will have to condense my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Rose, I would like to instruct you again that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom, III. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 18th of January, at 9.30 a.m. in this same courtroom, III.
